# Image saturation

- Route: `/tools/image-saturation`
- Kind: `tool`
- Category: `photo`
- Slug: `image-saturation`

## Summary

Vibrance for a boost that protects skin and already-strong colors, Saturation for a uniform scale, both as layers you can mask. (Photo editing)

## Details

Saturation is how far a color sits from gray at the same brightness. The Color group in the Basic panel of Aperture has two sliders for it, and the difference between them is the whole point of this page. Saturation multiplies every pixel's distance from its luma by the same factor, 1 + saturation / 100, so +50 pushes a pale pastel and a neon sign by the same proportion and the neon clips first. Vibrance scales that distance by a factor that shrinks as the color gets more saturated, 1 + v times (1 - range) where range is the gap between the largest and smallest channel, so muted colors move a lot, strong colors move a little, and a neutral gray does not move at all. Vibrance runs first, then Saturation, in one layer that can be masked to a color range or a subject.
### What it does
- Vibrance from -100 to +100: a saturation-aware boost or cut. For a positive value the factor is 1 + v times (1 - range), so a muted color with a channel range of 0.08 gets almost the full boost while a vivid color with a range of 0.63 gets about a third of it.
- Saturation from -100 to +100: every channel moves away from (or toward) the BT.709 luma of the pixel by the factor 1 + saturation / 100; -100 is a perfect gray conversion using the weights 0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722.
- Both sliders live in one Vibrance / saturation layer, so one opacity, one blend mode and one mask cover the pair; add a second layer if you want different masks for each.
- Skin protection comes free from the vibrance formula: a typical skin tone has a channel range near 0.3, so Vibrance +50 gives it about 70 percent of the saturation boost that the same value gives a near-gray.
- For color-specific control, the same page points you to the Color (HSL) panel, where each of six hue ranges has its own Saturation slider with width and feather.
### How to use it
1. Open the image: Drop the file. The Color group shows Vibrance and Saturation at 0 and the histogram shows the RGB channels.
2. Start with Vibrance: Raise it to +40 or +60. Muted areas such as foliage, water and fabric come up first; faces and already-bright colors barely change.
3. Add or subtract Saturation: A small Saturation change (+10 to +20, or -20 to -40 for a muted look) sets the overall level after Vibrance has balanced the colors.
4. Mask if needed, then export: Give the layer a Color range or Select subject mask to keep the change off one area, then export at full resolution.
### Supported formats
- Input: JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, HEIC, HEIF, AVIF, TIFF, BMP
- Output: JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, TIFF
- Heavy saturation boosts on a JPEG amplify chroma subsampling artifacts around red and blue edges; exporting as PNG or WebP at quality 95 or above avoids adding more.
- Saturation math is per pixel with no neighborhood, so export time is dominated by decoding and encoding rather than the adjustment.
### Technical details
- Vibrance: range = max(R, G, B) - min(R, G, B), l = the vibrance luma of the pixel (weights 0.072 red, 0.715 green, 0.213 blue, the ordering the underlying filter uses), factor f = 1 + v times (1 - sign(v) times range) with v = vibrance / 100; each channel becomes l + (channel - l) times f, clamped.
- Saturation: l = BT.709 luma (0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722); each channel becomes l + (channel - l) times (1 + saturation / 100), clamped. At -100 every channel equals l, so the result is the same gray as a luma-weighted black and white conversion.
- The sign term makes negative vibrance stronger on saturated colors: at -40 a neon pink of 255, 40, 180 (range 0.84) has a factor of 0.26 and drops to 130, 73, 110, while a wood brown of 160, 120, 80 (range 0.31) has a factor of 0.47 and only falls to 136, 117, 98.
- Neither slider changes a neutral pixel: when R = G = B the distance from luma is 0 and any factor leaves it at 0, so grays, blacks and whites are untouched at every setting.
- While you edit, the preview is drawn on your GPU (WebGL2) from a 1920 px copy of the photo; when you export, the file is rendered on our server from the original at full resolution with the same formulas, and the two agree within a small documented tolerance, a few 8-bit levels at most, with grain exact. Vibrance and Saturation are per-pixel, so in practice they match to the level.
- Because both steps clamp to 0 to 1, a large boost on a strong color clips one channel and shifts the hue slightly; switching the layer blend to Color keeps the original luma and only moves the chroma, which limits that drift.
### When not to use it
This page changes the strength of every color at once, so it is the wrong tool when only one color is the problem: a sky that needs more blue, or a face that needs less red, belongs in the Color (HSL) panel, where each hue range has its own saturation. If you want a photo that is gray except for one object, the color pop presets already do that. And if the colors look wrong rather than weak, start with white balance; saturating a photo with a cast only makes the cast stronger.
### Use cases
- Flat overcast landscape: Vibrance +60 then Saturation +10: foliage at 70, 110, 50 and water come up, the gray sky stays gray, and a hiker in a red jacket does not turn into a beacon.
- Portrait with too much color: Vibrance -30 calms a red jacket and blue background while the skin, which has a moderate channel range, keeps most of its warmth.
- Muted film look: Saturation -35 with Contrast -20 from the Light group and a Split toning layer gives the faded palette without a preset.
- Product on white: Saturation +20 under a Select subject mask boosts the item alone; the white background is neutral and would not have moved anyway, but the mask keeps shadows on it clean.
### FAQ
Q: When should I use Vibrance instead of Saturation?
A: Use Vibrance when the photo has people in it or already has one strong color: its boost shrinks as a color gets more saturated, so skin at a channel range of about 0.3 gets roughly a third less than a muted gray-green. Use Saturation when you want every color to move by the same proportion, such as a uniform desaturation for a muted style.
Q: Does Saturation -100 give a proper black and white?
A: It gives a luma-weighted gray using the BT.709 weights, which is a reasonable default. The Black & white panel is better when you want to control how each color converts: its six channel sliders default to 40, 60, 40, 60, 20 and 80 and can darken a blue sky or lighten foliage in the conversion.
Q: Why does a strong color change hue when I push saturation?
A: Because the result is clamped at 0 and 1 per channel. A red of 200, 40, 40 at Saturation +50 becomes 255, 23, 23: the red channel hit the ceiling while the others kept falling, so the ratio between channels changed. Switch the layer blend to Color or use a smaller value to limit it.
Q: Will gray or white areas pick up a color cast?
A: No. A pixel with equal channels is already at its luma, and multiplying a zero distance by any factor gives zero, so neutrals stay neutral at every slider position in both directions.
Q: Can I saturate just one color, like the sky?
A: Two ways. Add a Color range mask to this layer with the eyedropper on the sky, or open the Color (HSL) panel and raise Saturation on the Blues range alone. The HSL route also lets you set the width and feather of the range.
Q: Is a saturation change visible in the exported file at full size?
A: Yes, identically: the server applies the same two formulas per pixel to the original, and because they contain no blur or neighborhood step the export matches the preview to within an 8-bit level.

## Routing

When to send a visitor here: Use when someone wants colours stronger or weaker across the whole photo: Vibrance boosts muted colours while protecting skin and vivid ones, Saturation scales all evenly, and -100 gives a grey conversion. Typical asks: "make colours pop", "tone down colours".
When to send them elsewhere: For one colour only (bluer sky, less red face) use Adjust image hue (adjust-image-hue) with its per-range sliders. To keep one colour and grey the rest use Color pop (color-pop). If the colours look wrong rather than weak use White balance (white-balance-photo).
Related tools: color-pop (keep one colour only); adjust-image-hue (per-colour hue and saturation); white-balance-photo (fix a cast first); black-and-white-photo (full monochrome)
